displayTitle: 2026-08-05 - Social Services and Community Committee - 2026/08/05 - SSC

chunks.text: Okay. You going well? Yeah. Morning, and welcome to the Mana Wāhine Ministry for Women long-term insights briefing. So thank you for coming, talking to the Social Services and Community Select Committee this morning. And it's fine, it's all to you, leader. Great. Thank you, Chair. Good morning, everyone.

It's great to be here this morning. Are you comfortable if I say a few opening remarks and then- Please do...hand over for discussion? Fantastic. So yeah, lovely to be here with you to talk about our long-term insights briefing, Free to Lead: Tackling the Effects of Online Harm on the Pipeline of Future Women Leaders. I'm Kelly Coombs, Chief Executive of the Ministry for Women, and I'm joined by members of my team, Anna Chalmers, who's the Deputy Secretary, Engagement, Policy and Delivery, Mel Pearson, who is our Engagement

and Communications Manager, and also Kylie Fletcher, who leads our Mana Wāhine Kaupapa inquiry, is joining us online as well. So this briefing looks ahead at an issue that's already shaping the conditions for women's participation and leadership and their safety in our digital age. We chose to focus on women in leadership because women's representation in this sphere is crucial to achieving gender equality.

A key feature of that briefing is the voice and perspectives of women, including young women. Their experience show how online harm is already shaping participation, influencing aspirations, and also the choices that young women are making about leadership, which can bring you into the spotlight in public life.

We are already seeing the impact of online abuse, threats, harassment, and the impact this has on discouraging women and girls from being visible, speaking up, sharing their points of view and perspectives on issues, or pursuing leadership roles. Women often experience online harm differently to men, with the abuse more likely to be gendered, sexualized, appearance-focused, or directed at their credibility and their right to speak.

These attacks can feel deeply personal and are often intended not to just criticize a view, but to intimidate, shame, or silence women from participating publicly. We wanted this long-term insights briefing to be future-focused, but also grounded in the Ministry's strategic priorities.

This briefing connects to our representation and leadership strategic focus area, as well as our safety one. Looking over the longer term, this is about setting women up for success by ensuring the environments they participate in, including online spaces, are safe, enabling, and do not place disproportionate barriers in the way of women's leadership.

The briefing doesn't make recommendations. Instead, it pulls together evidence, stakeholder insights, the perspectives and experience of women to put a broader conversation about what needs to change so that women and girls can participate confidently in public life, both now and in the future. Thank you.

Thank you very much. I'll take the first one. You can. Thank you. Really interesting report, and very concerning, to be honest. But I see that there's a section in here around the social trends globally towards women and how that's obviously driving the algorithms. Can you just elaborate a little bit further on your findings there and kind of what you're seeing from that perspective?

Certainly. So in terms of global trends, a couple of years ago, online harm and technology was a focus at the UN Commission on the Status of Women. So this is definitely not an issue that we're experiencing on our own. It's something that's very front of mind in these international gatherings when we're focused on gender equality.

And it's a conversation also about different ways in which this could be reshaped. So some of the themes that come up there are the importance of growing the pipeline of women and girls into STEM training, but particularly engineering and mathematics, so that they are involved in developing future technologies, and also the importance of having women at the governance tables of these companies that are leading the way in terms of technology and innovation.

So that's part of the conversation there. But absolutely, the impact that the online world is having on women's ability to participate and owning that leadership role is something that we are experiencing globally. In New Zealand, every two years, a survey's undertaken by the National Council of Women, and I think some of the key findings of that survey speaks to the points that you're making in your question also.

So, on the whole, that survey finds that 79% of New Zealanders agree that gender equality is a fundamental right. But within that, 60% of those surveyed still believe that sexism is an issue. And when you're looking at the younger demographic, young men, so in the 18 to 24-year-old cohort, are over twice as likely as young women to believe that gender equality has gone too far. And again, that is a trend that we're seeing happening in other like-minded

countries in terms of some shifting views. Mm. Tenders. Can I just hop on that? So, just in terms of those algorithms and what we're seeing globally and the target on women, do you feel that there needs to be some kind of responsibility because the big tech companies are obviously driving some of those algorithms- Yeah... towards women? I mean, are men experiencing the same targeting that we're seeing, not just in New Zealand, but in other countries around the world?

Mm. So I think definitely the type of experience of women and girls online is different. Mm. And I was at an event, I think it was last year, that the speaker hosted where we had a panel of MPs, and on that panel, men and women, and that was acknowledged by the men on the panel that for them, their experience is that their ideas will be tested or challenged-... but less personal, whereas all of the women MPs on the panel, their experience was quite different, that it was targeted to them as a woman, and it wasn't actually about their ideas or point of view.

In terms of what we heard through this research was that the women and the girls who we engaged with on the process, they talked about wanting to see greater responsibility and accountability from platforms. So that was their perspective. They also spoke from their point of view about having stronger laws and protections in place.

But also keeping up with technology, which I think, as we all appreciate, is quite challenging because it's so rapid in its advancement. A concept around having safer spaces by design, and we can talk to you a bit more about that if that's of interest.

Better education in digital literacy and clearer reporting pathways to support people where they're affected by online harm. They were some of the key themes that came through. As well as the importance for young women, in particular, to see role models.

So to see women in the public space expressing their point of views, holding leadership roles that they could look up to. Mel, you might want to talk a little bit more about that. Yeah. So from the young women and girls who engaged with us as part of this process, they were largely in that 16 to 25 age group.

And for them, when they spoke about algorithms and mis and disinformation online, they really shared that they would appreciate more education. So, how do you fact check something online? What do you do when things go wrong? And so for them, they placed a large emphasis on that early education on digital literacy in schools in particular.

Mm. They also spoke a lot about having safe spaces for them to share and connect online. Mm. The online world is a big area for them to socialize, for education, for example. And so they just spoke about having places where they can connect that are safe, and they know what to do to escalate things when they go wrong.

A key driver for us too, in our safety work more generally in terms of the work we've done with Netsafe, we called it Free to Lead. So resources for women to keep them owning their space, and doing it in a safe way to support employers to be looking after their employees. But it is really, we don't want women to step back from the online world because it's so critical to our lives, and it creates a lot of social and economic opportunities for women. So that's sort of something we think about also in our work more generally in this space.

And that is also another theme that comes up internationally. It's that some of the experiences that women are having, it can silence them. It can make them choose to retreat or to maybe not go for that leadership role that they had aspirations for. So that is something we're very mindful of, is how to make the space work, the online space work, because it's fundamental.

Well, just something interesting off something you said in your first answer around encouraging young women and girls into STEM subjects, and so they can actually help design these technologies that shape the future, basically. I'll share a brief, quick anecdote. I visited United Machines in Dunedin with Finance Minister Nicola Willis about a week and a half ago or something.

And the CEO and co-owner, a lady called Sarah Ramsay, who's also the chair of United, what have they got? Advanced Manufacturing Aotearoa. And a lot of people probably don't know these kind of stories. Mm. How do we help get these stories out so young women, younger girls can say, "These are people who are actually leading advanced technology right now." And New Zealand's have really, really exciting stuff that they're doing. Of course, you have advanced aerospace, medical technology, et cetera. And it's quite awesome.

But how do we get those stories out there more effectively? Any sort of thoughts on that? Yeah. That's a really good point. I think one of the really interesting areas that came up through the report was opportunities to influence and needing to get more women and girls into this space. Mm. So key to this, one of the potential areas is safety by design, which is where systems are much more designed with women in mind, women users. But in terms of that STEM piece, that's really important for the development end.

So we're particularly seeing that with the rapid advancement of AI, artificial intelligence, at the moment. So if you look at STEM numbers- There are on one level, more women are in STEM, but that's because a large variety of them are in healthcare. When you actually start to drill down and you look at ICT, we're looking at around 30%, but certainly not at the senior management levels as well.

And that's where that STEM representation, that representation of women, is quite vital to drive that. So absolutely, one of the roles of the ministry is to share those stories and make sure that we're promoting that work. That's definitely what we do through our channels and through our promotion of work, and how we've started to develop some of those more deliverable pieces to look into that space. But yes, no, I hear you.

You can't be what you can't see. Mm. And sharing those examples is a really good way of showing women that they can get into that space, and that we have a role in helping drive that. Mm. That through. I think in a way, also, our strategic outcome areas are quite interconnected. So safety is sort of that foundation that all women need to succeed. And when we've been doing our gender pay gap engagements across the country, we've met with some really interesting businesses, just like the one you mentioned.

I remember a very long-standing engineering business in Dunedin. And so kind of on the surface you might think, how many women would be there? What would the career pathways be? But they're doing excellent work. So we'll continue to look at excellent work in terms of creating pathways, getting women into engineering and into leadership.

So we will continue to look for opportunities where we can, yeah, really share those stories and really amplify those experiences and put everything out on the table. Another thing I thought was quite reassuring was in the gender attitude survey that I mentioned earlier. One of the perspectives or one of the things that they look at there, is sort of that differentiation between occupation of men and occupation of women. And the large majority of New Zealanders believe that roles, fields of study, et cetera,

should be open to men and women. So we've got that as the strong foundation here, but telling those stories, I think continues to be really important. Okay. That's helpful. Okay. So just what you raised there, that can go overnight. I had a woman who, she's come from Afghanistan.

She was a family violence judge there. We airlifted her out. For her, that became a pathway that just was impossible overnight in a society. And there are a whole lot of people trapped in that society who just cannot meet their potential whatsoever, because the society's changed. Now with our online developments, there's trends out there that are just completely misogynistic- Mm... that say women are to be trad wives, and there are people buying into that kind of narrative.

Did you look at that, the fragility of the image of leadership for when they're, and what sort of pushback we could organize? I'm particularly interested in the education issue, and with men, with boys, young men. Mm. Yeah. Just picking up on that last point, I think allies and allyship is something that's really important, and it's something that we are bringing into our work. So, the resources that we developed on the gender pay gap, many of those stories have male business owners talking about what they're doing to

understand, take action, address the gender pay gap in their organization. So, we've talked about really wanting to make sure that the contribution of men and the role that men can play in gender equality is something that's a feature of our work and how we think about it.

The reason why we focused on this for our long-term insights briefing, in part it's because we've got this fantastic pipeline that's been developed over time of women who are wanting to step into governance roles. So we've got around 1,100 women on our Board Connector database.

So that's fantastic. We've got that sitting there. The environment they move into needs to be one that works for them to, like you said, meet their potential, deliver on their aspirations. So we felt it was very important that we don't just think about building the pipeline, but we're also thinking about that broader environment, and that's the contribution that we wanted this briefing to make.

Like I said, it's sort of not offering solutions, but we can share the ideas and what the aspirations are of the women that we engaged with as part of this process. I might just, we're just going short on time. Sorry. I'll just Sorry. Yeah, my question is really about, there's obviously no recommendations or potential solutions in the briefing.

So we are too mixed in what cross-agency work are you doing, to look for those solutions, because I think everybody actually knows the problem. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Like it's really obvious right now. Yeah. So it's more just, I think the biggest thing that everyone grapples with is how to deal with the issues- Mm... and what the solution is. So have you guys, do you have a second part of this work plan or are you working with others?

Ministries- Yeah... around that? So it's a bit of both. So work we're leading on our own and work we're connecting in with others. So to give you a sense of some of the other work that's being explored that we may be able to contribute to, we've got close connections into the classifications office.

So currently they're thinking about whether they repeat some research that they did looking into misogyny, and we'd be able to work alongside them to support that. They've also got some work under develop, which is looking at, picking up on your point, a lot of this is knowing, but, looking at whether there's different trends and things coming through that we need to keep up with in terms of the rapid pace of change.

We've already got an established relationship with Netsafe. One of the bits of work that we're picking up post our Free to Lead work is working more with people who moderate our social media pages so that we're supporting them in their roles as moderators, which can also make the space better for women and girls.

Mm-hmm. And also connecting in with Ministry of Education in terms of the work that they're leading on digital literacy. So there's a lot of points of contact for us to make there. In terms of what we're doing, it was two weeks ago, we did some follow-up work to the stalking legislation, so I brought a copy along just because it's so new.

We worked with Human Resources New Zealand and Shine to develop a practical resource for employers off the back of the stalking legislation, so that they can kind of support their people who may be experiencing that. So we'll continue to bring that focus on women's economic empowerment and safety and see where the gaps are that we think we can add. So it's sort of contributing from the system perspective, and then being quite practical about what are the things that we can do to make a difference, to make sure these spaces are working for women and girls.

Supplementary, Cassandra. Yeah, I had a supplementary on that because I think it's a really good point. Obviously we need to look at solutions and where to go, because I suppose if I look at, as a female public figure, and the comments, they are so unacceptable, some of the comments that you get.

And I think as public figures, we kind of go, "Oh, well, we're in the public, so we just accept that." But what do you think we should be doing when we get these really misogynist, terrible, abusive- Threatening... comments that are on our feeds? I'm sure other female members here are experiencing the same, but I feel that it's getting worse, it's on the rise, and- Absolutely... we just become more accepting because social media is obviously a platform to be able to kind of get your message out there and get your narrative out there.

But I think the response from some people around the country is just horrifying. Yeah. Maybe I can make some comments on that and then hand over to Anna to take a touch on some new tools that have been developed that support that. So, firstly, what we hear from women is it's so important for you as leaders to be holding your roles and in those roles, because they can see you there, it grows their aspiration, and they want to follow in your footsteps. Last week I met with the visiting delegation of MPs from across the Pacific, in

the parliamentary exchange that was happening, and I was on a panel alongside a member of Parliamentary Services who's focused on all of your security. So, he was able to share some of the specific things that happen in our context, and I guess with thinking forward about how they might be relevant in other settings. But the message is really clear, that if woman MPs, if woman political leaders, journalists, business leaders aren't visible, that creates big issues. But absolutely how your safety and wellbeing is managed as part of that is really critical.

Because that's also what young women are looking at. They're looking at you all and seeing the impact that it might be having on you personally, the impact that it might be having on your families and your children, and that can have a really chilling impact on their ambition, where they think that they can contribute.

I'll hand over to Anna just to talk about some other things we've learnt about some tools that maybe can support you and others when you're facing these unacceptable comments and abuse. Yeah, just would agree with that. And obviously, there is no single solution, which is actually part of the biggest challenge here.

This has been an interesting meeting over in Paris with the OECD, looking at this digital transformation and actually some of the really challenging impacts for women in particular in office, and it's come up with very similar findings around, New Zealand is absolutely not alone, and that this rise is rapid. And so that any solutions need to be multifaceted and involve a range of people, including the service providers obviously themselves. And that really, taking that safety by design, and really working with them. But that needs a concerted effort.

We look a lot to Australia and the e-commissioner over there for some of the work that they are doing, which is leading in this space. I suppose more locally, there are some initiatives that have been developed. One's called Face Forward. It's a recent development which we are supporting as a ministry, and helping to support to be introduced across leading public figures in New Zealand.

It's free for use, and it is basically a technology that blocks these sorts of comments, and people are starting to use it to quite a lot of success. So that's something that we would really encourage and support, and really happy to share access into the people at Oreto Labs that are doing that work at the moment.

But look, yes, watch this space, because it is something that we really need to be focused on, and I think this is the opportunity with this outcome, is to also help to share and bring some people together that can look at it in a more concerted way as well. Unfortunately, results from the last year's local body elections did show a decline in women representatives at the table, and that, for the ministry, is really key because, as you say, these gains for women's representation have been hard-fought.

So it's how do we come together and really work to try and not make it such a challenging and terrible environment for people in that public office, as well as the safety aspects to it. Commissioner Warren. I do. Thank you. It is a bit of a sop to that, but I had two questions. My other one was about the survey that you did.

Did you notice, or did you track the difference between urban and rural in terms of the impact some of this is having? So I'll leave that one with you. But I just want to pick up on the conversation that we've been having. And it always seems to me, maybe because I've got a few summers behind me, that- Don't worry... I always hear that it's somebody else's problem to solve.

Yeah. And from my point of view, picking up on what Catherine said about the comments- Mm... I don't get that on my social media feed. Yeah. And the reason is because if someone says anything negative-... I block them. Mm-hmm. Problem solved. And so, we tend to think about the issues as being someone else's issue. But actually, what's going on that people can't do a simple thing like turn their phone off or block people that say things you don't like? It's very simple.

Yeah. What's going on here? It makes me think of when we did our Behind the Keyboard series, which was when we had women telling their stories, women with a public profile and really wanting to get these issues out there. I remember one of the women talked about posting and ghosting. So, to say your piece, but then not to just- Mm.

The way she kept herself safe was just to not look at the comments. Or she did her thing, and she moved on to the next thing. Yes. So I just think it might've been something, too, that could be a little bit generational. Mel, I'm not sure if from our engagement with young women, whether they had a different point of view on that.

Yeah. I think what came through engagement is, particularly for women with a public profile, there's a lot of that lower threshold harm coming through. So those consistent comments. So they might not be at the level where you think, "Oh, this is actually really serious, and I need to take action," but they're quite consistent.

So that's what we heard is happening online quite a bit. And so there are tools and things that young women have used, and women in leadership have used alongside blocking. But when people are moderating their pages, there are options that you can set up pages to work for you.

So in our Free to Lead toolkit, there's guidance around the spaces you choose to be in, and you get to set the tone. So there's things like creating community guidelines and making it really clear, the people who are interacting with you, what you'll expect, and what you'll put up with. And what we heard through some of the engagement is that there is a lot of self-censorship after that takes place.

So, once somebody has put on their page, "I'm going to talk about X, Y, Z. I won't be taking commentary around my identity," or whatever that looks like, there's a lot of self-moderation. And when those rules were in place, people noticed a drop in some of that harmful commentary.

Yeah. Because what you find too, Mr. Chair, is that if you don't kick those comments out, those negative ones out, it then puts off people actually trying to make positive contributions. Mm. Mm. Yes. And so, it's almost self-fulfilling. Yes. So, they end up with the voice.

Yes. And so I don't tolerate it. But I'm listening to you ladies talk about the toolkits and all this, but it just seems so simple to me. Because we are in control. Mm-hmm. And we're trying to make- But once it's there, it's there. Yeah. Yes, you can hide it, you can block them.

But when you're getting a barrage of hundreds and hundreds of comments coming at you, yes, keep blocking, but the point is that they're making those comments, and they're coming at you. Well, you can't stop other people from commenting. No, of course you can't. Of course you can't. You can't. Oh, I'd like to make a last question, and then we might ad journal. No, I'm enjoying the conversation. I think it's a real one.

I think it's the way in which we should approach this, because I think so recently, threats were made, and then the guy turned up out on the forecourt, and I just wanted to go out and just drop him. Now-... that's just the real me. Yeah. And I think what Catherine's saying, in our own ways, we're dealing with these things, in our own way, I guess.

But I guess, and I think about that, and then I'm noticing the words I've circled, which is, when you opened up, you talked about online harm, abuse, threat, Free to Lead, safety by design. Mm. See, already we're positioned in the back. Mm. We're positioned behind the ball, and we're not- And that's leadership, but it's this not full out and lead, and there's no one else in the room.

Yeah. I'm the only leader in the room. Mm-hmm. We don't get to that privilege yet. I think it is a generational too. Sorry, my girlfriend says I'm good. I think it is a generational thing. I think there's this digital immigrant versus digital native. Mm-hmm. And I think that's also part of what you- Mm-hmm... witness when you're doing your work.

But what's my question? Actually, I don't even know I've got one. I think there's a range of answers that already exist inside of each of us, which I think I wouldn't mind. You wouldn't want to say, "Look, just go out and drop them." Even though there's something in that idea of taking it in our own hands.

And I know people get like, "Well, you can't just..." People get nervous about women particularly wanting to be so proactive and so ordinary about being able to protect ourselves online, at home, in our stores, at our clubs, wherever we happen to live. So I don't know whether any of where you're working goes to that real end where the real harm exists.

Mm-hmm. When you talked about misogyny, and we're doing some work around that, and I'm like, "It's as plain as hell. We're screwed by it." Mm-hmm. And it is evident everywhere we work. Mm-hmm. So I didn't really get to my question, did I? No, it's a good round. I don't even know why I brought it. It's okay. I totally agree. But you did raise- A discussion. Yeah. I think that it's a point well made in terms to of some of the language, and fundamental for our work and how we want to position it is to empower women- Yep

... through information, through tools, through connections, through communities, through storytelling. Yeah. Mm-hmm. I teach, and I still teach self-defense to women and girls. I've been teaching it for more than 35 years now. Mm-hmm. And across the country, actually.

And the stories that I hear from those women, and they're professional women, they're non-professional women, and girls, and young girls, and kids in school, and this is more than 30 or 40 years. I just don't see the progress that I wish- Mm-hmm... I would expect to see.

I would expect to see. I don't get it. Mm-hmm. So yeah. I know what I'm going to be doing. I'm just going to be teaching more self-defense, both in your mind and in your body. Be able to protect yourself wherever you are. Mm-hmm. Good. Because I- Well, that fits in well with- Can I just wrap that up? I did a speech in the House about this once- Mm... a few years ago, and the only place that a bully can survive is when they've got a victim.

So we've got to stop making women victims. Um- Which is what you're doing. Public semester answer. Sorry. I've got a thing next Tuesday, which is a movie on strangulation. Mm. Mm. You are all absolutely welcome to come to it. It is a documentary, and it's the first showing of it.

That's wonderful. That's true of the whole committee. I know it's tangential, but I think it's in the- It's in the diary. Yeah. Thank you. Thank you. Well, thank you very much for coming in and having a great discussion this morning. No, that's great. Appreciate it. You too. Thank you, everyone. Thank you. Thank you.
